Pericardiocentesis relieves tamponade as a temporising measure; definitive repair is by sternotomy or thoracotomy in theatre. ED thoracotomy is for traumatic arrest.
As well as measuring oxygen saturation, a pulse oximeter also gives useful information regarding what other factor in the initial assessment of the traumatised patient?
The plethysmographic trace and a reliable signal depend on pulsatile flow, so a poor trace indicates poor peripheral perfusion; oximetry gives no CO2 or acid–base information.

A 30-year-old man with a pelvic fracture is hypotensive and tachycardic. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.24, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3− 14 mmol/L and base deficit −10. What is the most appropriate management of his acid–base derangement?

Lactic (metabolic) acidosis from hypoperfusion is corrected by restoring circulating volume and perfusion; bicarbonate does not treat the cause and may worsen intracellular acidosis.

A low wedge pressure with tachycardia and oliguria after AAA repair means hypovolaemia, so a crystalloid bolus is given; diuretics or vasodilators would worsen it.

A 70-year-old man is given IV fluids for hypovolaemia after AAA repair. Several hours later his BP is 150/85 mmHg with distended neck veins and an elevated pulmonary wedge pressure, and urine output remains low. What is the next step?
IV furosemide|A bolus of IV crystalloid|A dopamine infusion|A nitroprusside infusion|IV digoxin
Hypertension with high filling pressures and poor output after fluid loading responds to afterload reduction with nitroprusside, improving cardiac output and renal perfusion.

She is in haemorrhagic shock, so blood volume is restored first, then the placenta is removed manually; with a firm fundus, uterotonics or packing for atony will not help.

A patient is admitted following a motorcycle accident. He has fractured his left femur, tibia, fibula and pelvis. His blood pressure is 70/35 mmHg, pulse 140 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min and Glasgow Coma Scale score 9/15. You wish to resuscitate the patient. Which one of the following procedures may be contraindicated in such a patient?
A pelvic fracture may tear the urethra, so a urethral catheter is avoided until urethral injury is excluded (blood at meatus, retrograde urethrogram).

A patient is admitted following an assault. On assessment, he has a stab wound to his chest. Clinically, he has a massive haemothorax and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 4/15. Without further management, this patient will succumb to which cause of death first?
Which of the following techniques does not provide a definitive airway?
A definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea (oro/nasotracheal, surgical); a laryngeal mask sits above the larynx and does not protect against aspiration.

A patient is admitted following a road traffic accident. He has sustained significant blunt injury to his head, chest and abdomen and has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8/15. His saturations are poor at 89% on 15 L of oxygen via a non-rebreathing mask. You note bruising around both eyes and blood-stained fluid issuing from his left ear, which forms concentric rings when dripped on a white sheet. You wish to support his airway to improve oxygenation. The first choice of airway adjunct would be:
Raccoon eyes and CSF otorrhoea suggest a basal skull fracture, so a nasopharyngeal airway is avoided; an oropharyngeal airway is used pending a definitive airway.

A 35-year-old butcher is admitted after inadvertently stabbing himself with a knife. His airway is patent and there is no identifiable hindrance to breathing. His pulse is 110 beats/min, BP 130/105 mmHg and respiratory rate 25 breaths/min. Assuming a body mass of 70 kg, what is the best estimate of the volume of blood lost?
Tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure and RR 25 with normal systolic BP is class II shock (15–30% loss, 750–1500 mL in a 70 kg adult), i.e. about 1000 mL.

A homeless man is admitted unresponsive after being found by police on a park bench. He has no external signs of injury. An oesophageal temperature probe records his core body temperature to be 34 °C. Which of the following management options is not routinely indicated in this case?
At 34 °C (mild hypothermia) passive and active external rewarming with warmed IV fluids suffice; invasive core rewarming such as peritoneal lavage is for severe hypothermia.

Hypotension with a very low ejection fraction (15%) and high CVP in a patient with coronary disease is cardiogenic shock (pump failure, probably perioperative MI).
Salmon-coloured (serosanguinous) wound discharge on day 3 heralds fascial dehiscence, so the wound is explored and the abdomen closed in theatre.

A 65-year-old diabetic man develops spiking fever on the 6th day after laparotomy for duodenal ulcer, with incisional discomfort and a small amount of wound drainage. Appropriate evaluation and management should include which of the following?
A superficial wound infection is treated by opening the incision, sending pus for culture and local wound care; antibiotics only if there is cellulitis or systemic sepsis.
A 40-year-old woman with a BMI of 45 kg/m² has an HbA1c of 7% (53 mmol/mol) and a fasting blood glucose of 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). What metabolic disorder does she have?
Insulin resistance with impaired glucose control (type 2 diabetes)
HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) confirm type 2 diabetes, driven by obesity-related insulin resistance.
A 40-year-old woman with a BMI of 45 kg/m² has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7%) despite lifestyle measures. What is the most appropriate surgical management of her metabolic disorder?
Bariatric (metabolic) surgery, e.g. sleeve gastrectomy
BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with comorbidity such as diabetes) qualifies for bariatric/metabolic surgery, which often induces remission of type 2 diabetes.

A 45-year-old man with a BMI of 37 kg/m² has a fasting blood glucose of 6.5 mmol/L (117 mg/dL) and an HbA1c of 6.2% (44 mmol/mol) on two occasions, despite 6 months of diet and exercise. Does he need any treatment for his blood sugar?
He has prediabetes (non-diabetic hyperglycaemia); if intensive lifestyle change fails, metformin reduces progression to diabetes, especially when BMI ≥35.

A 45-year-old obese man has fasting triglycerides of 600 mg/dL (6.8 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol 95 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) and HDL 38 mg/dL, despite 3 months of diet and exercise. Does he need any treatment for his lipid profile?
Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>500 mg/dL) with normal LDL risks pancreatitis and is treated with a fibrate when lifestyle measures fail; statins mainly lower LDL.

A lady underwent sleeve gastrectomy 2 days earlier. She presents with tachycardia and tachypnoea. Chest examination is normal. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness but normal-looking laparoscopic incisions. Gastrografin swallow shows contrast leaking from the staple line.
Tachycardia and tachypnoea after sleeve gastrectomy suggest a staple-line leak even with minimal abdominal signs; contrast extravasation confirms it.
Hypoxia, hypotension, raised JVP, trachea deviated to the left and a hyper-resonant silent right chest is a right tension pneumothorax: needle or finger decompression now.
Reduced GCS in a drinker without head injury or shock suggests hypoglycaemia (alcohol impairs gluconeogenesis): check capillary glucose as part of 'D' in the primary survey.
A penetrating left precordial wound with hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) is cardiac tamponade.

A 68-year-old man complains of increasing dysphagia of 3 months' duration and has lost 25 kg in weight. Endoscopic biopsy confirms oesophageal carcinoma and CT shows no metastases. Which investigation best assesses the local (T and N) stage?
Endoscopic ultrasound is the most accurate test for depth of oesophageal wall invasion (T) and regional nodes (N) once CT has excluded metastases.
Back pain in confirmed prostate cancer suggests bone metastases; a radionuclide (isotope) bone scan surveys the whole skeleton.
A painful, deformed ankle after injury is a suspected fracture-dislocation: plain X-ray (after urgent reduction if the foot is threatened).
A haemodynamically stable patient after blunt thoraco-abdominal trauma is best assessed by contrast-enhanced CT for solid-organ and vascular injury.
Intraoperative ultrasound of the liver detects small occult metastases and defines their relation to vessels during resection of colorectal liver metastases.
PET-CT is the standard staging investigation for lymphoma, showing metabolically active nodal and extranodal disease.
RUQ pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign suggest acute cholecystitis; ultrasound is the first-line investigation.
A hard, fixed, growing deep soft-tissue mass suggests sarcoma; MRI is the best test for local staging before core biopsy.
A femoral fracture with tachycardia, hypotension and flat neck veins after trauma means blood loss: hypovolaemic shock.
Sudden breathlessness, hypotension and erythema at the cannula site soon after IV drugs (e.g. antibiotics) suggests anaphylaxis.

A 68-year-old patient who had an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair was in significant pain postoperatively and was seen by the acute pain team about 15 minutes ago. His blood pressure has now dropped to 90/50 mmHg with a pulse of 60/min; he is slightly dizzy, though urine output is adequate and CVP is +12.
Hypotension with bradycardia and a normal CVP just after an epidural top-up reflects sympathetic blockade (neurogenic-type shock), not hypovolaemia.
Collapse with a rigid abdomen, fever and tachycardia suggests perforation with peritonitis causing septic shock.

Breathlessness with bibasal crackles in an elderly patient after several units is transfusion-associated circulatory overload: stop, sit up and give a diuretic.

Jaundice 5–10 days after transfusion is a delayed haemolytic reaction from an anamnestic antibody response to a minor red-cell antigen.
A 24-year-old patient is noted to be flushed a few minutes after starting a red cell transfusion; temperature is 37.8°C and observations are otherwise stable.
Isolated mild fever and flushing with stable observations is a non-haemolytic febrile reaction (cytokines/leucocyte antibodies): slow the transfusion and give paracetamol.

Small areas of frontal haemorrhage on CT after an assault with a slowly falling GCS (oedema around the bruise) is a cerebral contusion.
A crescentic (concave) hyperdense collection with fluctuating consciousness after a fall in an elderly patient is an acute subdural haematoma.
A 42-year-old man is found unconscious on the street with bruising around both eyes and a clear nasal discharge.
Bilateral periorbital (raccoon) bruising with CSF rhinorrhoea indicates an anterior basal skull fracture.
A 25-year-old was involved in a high-speed road traffic accident 48 hours ago. He has been comatose since the injury. There are no major abnormalities on CT.

Coma from the moment of a high-speed (acceleration–deceleration) injury with a near-normal CT is diffuse axonal injury; MRI shows the shearing lesions.

Respiratory distress, poor right-sided expansion, tracheal deviation to the left and distended neck veins is a right tension pneumothorax.
A 45-year-old patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with bruising all over the chest and exhibits shallow tachypnoea with indrawing of the chest wall.
Paradoxical indrawing of a chest-wall segment after blunt trauma is a flail chest (two or more ribs each broken in two places).
A 45-year-old man is stabbed in the right side of the chest. Chest X-ray shows a whiteout of the right lung field.

A penetrating chest wound with whiteout of the hemithorax on an erect film is a haemothorax: chest drain, thoracotomy if ≥1500 mL.

A 26-year-old man is brought to A&E in extremis after a single stab wound to the left side of the chest. He is tachypnoeic, heart sounds are muffled and blood pressure is 90/55 mmHg despite IV fluid resuscitation.
F
A left chest stab wound with muffled heart sounds and hypotension unresponsive to fluid is cardiac tamponade.
A red, swollen, tender groin wound 5 days after hernia repair is a surgical site infection, which typically appears 5–7 days postoperatively.
Massive tympanitic colonic distension without tenderness, an empty rectum and reduced bowel sounds after orthopaedic surgery is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie).
Low-grade pyrexia, tachycardia, hypoxia and reduced breath sounds at a base within 48 hours of laparotomy is basal atelectasis.
Sudden pain, fever, hypotension, peritonism and wound discharge 4 days after anterior resection is anastomotic leak (dehiscence).
Calf discomfort, low-grade fever and asymmetrical (right > left) ankle oedema a week after pelvic cancer surgery is deep vein thrombosis.
An ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area suggests aortic stenosis, which must be assessed by echocardiography before anaesthesia.
Poorly controlled asthma should be assessed with spirometry (peak flow/FEV1) and optimised before elective surgery.
Obstructive jaundice impairs vitamin K absorption, so a clotting screen (INR) is essential before ERCP and sphincterotomy.
Transient monocular blindness and arm weakness are TIA symptoms; carotid Doppler is needed to detect significant stenosis before cardiac surgery.
A tense, transilluminable swelling in which the testis cannot be felt separately is a hydrocele (scan the testis, as a tumour can cause a secondary hydrocele).
A lump arising from the testis in a young man with weight loss is a testicular tumour until proven otherwise: ultrasound and tumour markers.
A scrotal swelling one cannot get above, with a cough impulse and no transillumination, is an inguinoscrotal (indirect) hernia.
A left-sided 'bag of worms' that empties on lying down is a varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus).
